title: A Knight Is Enough: Complete the Queen Fork
summary: Capture the queen, then watch the blocked central pawns rather than treating the knight ending as already finished.

nodes.question: The knight fork is in place. Should White finish the capture?
nodes.explanation: Nd8 attacks Qf7, while Kc7 attacks the knight. Nxf7 removes the queen and reaches a winning seven-piece ending. The eight-piece root is proved by that legal winning capture, not directly queried in a tablebase.

branches.title: Source finish: collect the queen
commentary: Begin after ...Kc7, reconstructed between the saved 76-second Nd8/Kb7/Qf7 and 77-second Nf7/Kc7 diagrams. Earlier rook and knight offers remain outside this proof scope.

Nxf7 removes the queen and escapes the king’s attack. The exact seven-piece knight-and-pawn versus three-pawns ending is winning for White. This capture is a legal winning witness for the preceding eight-piece position; it does not prove the earlier nine-piece double offer.

branches.title: Independent continuation: watch the d-pawn
commentary: Continue independently after the source’s queen capture. These pawn and knight moves are representative checked analysis, not moves claimed to appear in the clip.
Nxf7 captures the queen and preserves a forced White win.
d3 advances Black’s passer, but White’s d2 pawn still blocks further forward progress. All three black pawns remain in the reconstruction.
Ne5 attacks d3 and centralizes the knight. White still wins, but further king and knight coordination is required; the lesson does not call this a finished conversion or a forced pawn capture.

exercises.prompt: Why does the queen capture prove this later position is winning?
exercises.answer: White has a legal move, Nxf7, whose complete resulting position is an exact Black loss. That establishes a White win without pretending the eight-piece root was directly tablebase-probed.

exercises.prompt: Why keep White’s d2 pawn in the reconstruction?
exercises.answer: It stops the black d-pawn’s forward progress on d3, giving White time to coordinate king and knight. Removing it would change the ending.
